name: Dull Citrine
lede: Dull Citrine is a grayed, olive-toned yellow-brown first plated by Robert Ridgway in 1912, and one of the more common colors in our whole painting archive.

sections.title: A modifier on an old fruit name
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* of 1912 plates this swatch at plate XVI, hue 21 prime, on an aged, scanned original that is itself approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 files the name in block 106, light olive [1]. The name pairs *dull* with [[citrine]], a word that first meant lemon yellow and later named the tertiary between orange and green [4].

At hex #8D8552 it measures lightness 55 and chroma 29 in LCH [1]. Its closest named neighbor is [[serpentine-green|Serpentine Green]], 2.8 units away and more vivid; [[buffy-citrine|Buffy Citrine]] sits 4.7 units off and yellower, and [[parrot-green|Parrot Green]] 4.8 units off, also yellower and brighter [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 6.57% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (1,562 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 853 [3]. In our archive it is more common than 88% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1700s, present in 4.9% of the 3,449 paintings we have from that century (169 paintings), 1.3 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 37% of the paintings where the within-painting lens finds it, by lightness rank [3]. Its most devoted painter is Arnoud van Halen, present in 21 of 50 works here, 6.3x the baseline of the museums those works come from (as photographed 4.0x) [3]. The earliest match dates to 916, 996 years before the name's 1912 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
